items.back: Jana (tribe) + Pada (feet) — the land where a tribe settled.

items.front: How many Mahajanapadas, and which texts list them?
items.back: 16; listed in Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and Mahavastu, plus Jain texts. Rise from 6th c. BCE.

items.front: Socio-economic drivers of the rise of Mahajanapadas?
items.back: Land replaced cattle as wealth; iron weapons; taxable agri-surplus; growth of towns. (Mnemonic LITT.)
items.examPoint: Rise of Mahajanapadas (6th c. BCE) & socio-economic causes

items.back: Vajji, Malla, Assaka — ruled by councils of clan reps. Founders of Jainism & Buddhism came from republics.
Capital Vaishali; run on the Sangha system — the most powerful republic.
Kosala–Shravasti, Vatsa–Kausambi, Kashi–Banaras (Varanasi). All in Uttar Pradesh.

items.front: North-western Mahajanapadas and their claims to fame?
items.back: Gandhara–Taxila (Silk Road, fusion art); Kamboja–Rajpur (famed for horses).

items.front: Which Mahajanapada lay south of the Vindhyas, and on which river?
items.back: Ashmaka (Assaka), capital Potana/Potali (Maharashtra), on the Godavari — the only Deccan one.
Kuru–Hastinapur (Mahabharata); Anga–Champa (invention of veena); Malla–Kushinara/Pava (Buddha's Mahaparinirvana).
items.examPoint: Eastern & Buddhist-linked capitals (Anga-Champa/veena, Malla-Kushinara/Pava, Videha-Mithila, Vajji-Vaishali)

items.back: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) pottery and punch-marked coins (India's earliest coinage).

items.front: Land tax rate and its name; the merchant guilds?
items.back: Bhaga = 1/6th of produce; Bali also levied; rich merchants = grihapatis, organised in sartha guilds.
items.examPoint: Economy & taxation — Bhaga (1/6th), Bali, grihapatis, sartha guilds

items.front: Key Mahajanapada officials: minister, commander, village head?
items.back: Mahamatras (ministers), Senanayaka (commander), Gramabhojaka/Gramini (village headman, collected tax).
items.examPoint: Administration & army — king, Mahamatras, Senanayaka, Gramabhojaka; village types

items.back: Fertile Ganga plains (rice), minerals & textile trade, military power under Bimbisara → India's first empire.

items.front: Early Vedic clans — way of life and prime political aim?
items.back: Pastoral, moving in search of grazing land; the aim was to control the best pasture lands.

items.front: What changed in the Later Vedic Period (1000–600 BCE)?
items.back: The Jana took up agriculture, settled permanently in Janapadas, which became state territories (Rashtra).
About 600–322 BCE — 6th century BCE to the rise of the Mauryas.

items.front: Jain text that lists sixteen Mahajanapadas (a different list)?
items.back: The Bhagavati Sutra; the standard list is in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya.

items.front: Assaka — capital's modern town and northern neighbour?
items.back: Potana/Potali = Bodhan (Telangana); the Godavari separated Assaka from Mulaka.
Kosala — wheat, barley, sugarcane, trade routes; Vatsa — culture and learning; Kashi — spirituality and learning, rice.
Chedi — valorous warriors; Matsya — named from fish (aquatic life); Panchala — Vedic rituals and scholarship.

items.front: Famous king of Vatsa in the Buddha's time?
items.back: Udayana, ruling from Kausambi.

items.front: Iron tools of the age and their effect?
items.back: Axes, adzes, sickles — allowed forest clearing and the spread of agriculture.

items.front: Two farming changes that raised output?
items.back: Iron ploughshares; transplanting paddy saplings instead of broadcasting seed — more yield but more labour.

items.front: Main crops of the Mahajanapada age?
items.back: Paddy, barley, cotton, pulses and sugarcane.

items.back: A chief (king) elected by the ruling clans, who governed with a council (Ganaparishad).
